documentation: kotlin.lang is a pseudo-package, not a real Kotlin one — these entries track core LANGUAGE SYNTAX (vararg, null-safety operators, class/control-flow constructs, destructuring) that has no real stdlib declaration id of its own, but is exactly the kind of 'what does this transpiler actually support' surface the user wants tracked here alongside the real kotlin.*/kotlin.collections.*/kotlin.math.*/kotlin.text.*/kotlin.ranges.* manifests.

declarations.name: vararg
declarations.implementation: Parser.kt parameter modifier, Emitter.kt (binds Lua's own ... into a table)
limitations: Only allowed on a function's last parameter (enforced with a clear parse error otherwise) — matches Kotlin's own rule here, not a real gap

declarations.name: spreadOperator
limitations: A spread *array argument is only valid in the last argument position — no mixing multiple spreads, no spreading into a non-last vararg slot. Matches Kotlin's own positional rule reasonably closely.

declarations.implementation: Ast.SafeChainExpr, Emitter.kt (IIFE stepping through a temp var with a nil short-circuit per step)

declarations.documentation: Deliberately emits an explicit ~= nil check rather than Lua's `a or b` idiom, since `or` would also treat Kotlin's `false` as 'absent'

declarations.name: ?: return
declarations.implementation: Ast.ReturnExpr detection on the Elvis's right side, Emitter.kt
declarations.documentation: Lowered as a guard statement rather than a nested IIFE-with-return
IIFE that errors with a message if the value is nil

declarations.name: class
limitations: Primary-constructor params must be val/var-prefixed (a bare non-property param is rejected); only fun/val/var members allowed in the body — no nested classes, no init blocks, no companion objects

declarations.name: classInheritance
limitations: Single-superclass only; open/override modifiers are parsed and ignored (relies on __index chain shadowing); no super.foo() calls at all — super is a hard unsupported keyword

declarations.name: interface
limitations: Hard unsupported keyword — raises a parse error immediately

declarations.name: enum class
limitations: Explicitly listed as an unsupported class modifier — raises a clear diagnostic

declarations.name: sealed class
limitations: Same as enum class — explicitly rejected with a clear diagnostic

declarations.name: abstract class
limitations: Same as enum/sealed class — explicitly rejected

declarations.name: companion object
limitations: object is only recognized as a top-level/standalone statement — there's no parsing path for a companion object nested inside a class body

declarations.name: object
declarations.documentation: Top-level singleton object Name { ... } compiles to a global (not local) Lua table, so plugin code across files can share it

declarations.name: data class
limitations: Only auto-generates a Kotlin-formatted __tostring (Point(x=1, y=2)) when the class doesn't define its own toString. Does NOT auto-generate a structural equals()/hashCode() — == on two data class instances with equal fields compiles to plain Lua == (reference identity), which is WRONG vs Kotlin's structural equality. componentN() isn't generated as a real callable method either (destructuring reads constructor-param order directly instead).

declarations.name: copy
limitations: Named-argument form only — a positional .copy(newX, newY) call isn't handled

declarations.name: equals
limitations: No structural equals()/hashCode() generated for a real user data class at all — a genuine correctness gap, distinct from the separate collection-key structural-equality mechanism (canonicalKeyStr/structuralEq), which only applies to externally-bound 'record' types, not user data classes

declarations.name: componentN()
limitations: Not generated as a real callable method on a user data class — only destructuring syntax (val (a, b) = x) reads the constructor-param order directly; calling .component1() explicitly is only supported for the separate externally-bound 'record' types

declarations.name: if (expression)
declarations.implementation: Emitter.kt (Lua's `cond and a or b` idiom)
limitations: Inherits the idiom's known falsy-branch bug if the true-branch value can itself be false/nil-equivalent

declarations.name: when (expression)
declarations.implementation: WhenFeature.kt, WhenEmitter.kt (IIFE with explicit return per branch)
limitations: Requires an else branch — no exhaustiveness checking against sealed/enum types (which aren't supported anyway)

declarations.name: when (is Type)
limitations: Only Int/Double/String/Boolean type checks — no real RTTI/class checks against user types

declarations.name: do-while
limitations: No DoWhile AST node, no parser path at all

declarations.name: try-catch-finally
limitations: At most one catch total, not per exception type (the catch param's declared type is parsed and discarded); try cannot be used as an expression; a bare return inside the try body returns from the pcall wrapper closure, not the enclosing function

declarations.name: throw
limitations: Throwing an unregistered exception type throws just the string message, no real exception hierarchy; throwing a declared class instance throws that table value, catchable as-is

declarations.name: break
limitations: Hard unsupported keyword, even though Lua itself has a native break

declarations.name: continue
limitations: Hard unsupported keyword

declarations.name: break@label / continue@label
limitations: Moot since unlabeled forms are already rejected; no @label syntax exists at all

declarations.name: non-local return from a lambda
declarations.implementation: Emitter.kt (forEach/map/filter lambdas inline directly into a real Lua for loop)
limitations: Works correctly, but only by accident, for inlined iteration lambdas (forEach/map/filter/...); a return inside a genuine closure-call lambda (let/run/also/apply/with) returns only from that inner Lua function, not a real Kotlin-style non-local return. No return@label qualified-return syntax exists.

declarations.name: val (a, b) = expr
limitations: For a tracked user class, reads declared constructor properties in order (not real componentN() calls); for anything else, assumes a Pair-like shape via .first/.second and supports exactly 2 names — no Triple type exists at all, and 3+ names on an untracked value fails loudly at runtime

declarations.name: { (k, v) -> }
limitations: Only works for a Map-entry lambda parameter (which passes key+value as two real args already) — not a generic 'destructure any Pair-shaped single lambda arg into two names' feature

declarations.name: for ((k, v) in map)
limitations: Only ever 2 names (the Map-entry case) — no 3+-name for-loop destructuring
